identity.title: Pulsus paradoxus >10-12 mmHg (inspiratory SBP fall by manual cuff)

technique.how: With the patient breathing normally, inflate a manual cuff above SBP and deflate slowly (2-3 mmHg/beat). Note the pressure at which Korotkoff sounds are first heard only in expiration, then the pressure at which they are heard throughout the respiratory cycle; the difference is the pulsus. >10 mmHg is abnormal.
technique.prerequisites: Manual sphygmomanometer and stethoscope; regular rhythm; quiet, unlaboured breathing (deep breathing exaggerates the fall). A pulse-oximeter plethysmograph or arterial line can substitute.
technique.contraindications: Unreliable in atrial fibrillation, marked tachypnea, or when the patient cannot breathe steadily.

interpretation.positive_finding: In a patient with a known pericardial effusion, pulsus >10 mmHg raises the likelihood of tamponade (LR 3.3) and is present in about 82% of tamponade cases. In acute asthma a large pulsus tracks severity of airflow obstruction.
interpretation.negative_finding: Pulsus <=10 mmHg in a patient with a pericardial effusion makes tamponade much less likely (LR 0.03, single study). Absence of pulsus does not exclude severe asthma.
interpretation.pitfalls: Pulsus is also produced by severe asthma/COPD, massive PE, obesity and hypovolemia, and can be absent in tamponade with LV dysfunction, ASD, aortic regurgitation or positive-pressure ventilation. Studies were done in patients already known to have effusions, so LRs do not apply to undifferentiated dyspnea.
interpretation.changes_what: Pulsus >10 mmHg with known effusion: treat as probable tamponade, urgent echo/pericardiocentesis; <=10 mmHg argues strongly against it.

estimates.target_condition: Cardiac tamponade in patients with pericardial effusion (pulsus paradoxus >10 mmHg)
estimates.population: Patients with known pericardial effusion referred for pericardiocentesis or with suspected tamponade (single study)
estimates.reference_standard: Tamponade diagnosed by echocardiography/hemodynamics at pericardiocentesis
estimates.quote: 3.3; 95% CI, 1.8-6.3), while a pulsus paradoxus of 10 mm Hg or less greatly lowers the likelihood (likelihood ratio, 0.03; 95% CI, 0.01-0.24)

estimates.target_condition: Cardiac tamponade (presence of pulsus paradoxus among patients with tamponade)
estimates.population: Patients with known tamponade or referred for pericardiocentesis with known effusion; 8 studies

estimates.target_condition: Severe acute asthma requiring admission or relapse (pulsus paradoxus >15 mmHg at 30 min, continuous non-invasive measurement)
estimates.population: Children with acute asthma, urban pediatric ED (continuous non-invasive PP measurement, not manual cuff)
estimates.reference_standard: Masked disposition decision (admission for further treatment) or relapse
estimates.quote: the sensitivity was 0.42, the specificity was 0.89, and the likelihood ratio was 3.86

sources.citation: Roy CL, Minor MA, Brookhart MA, Choudhry NK. Does this patient with a pericardial effusion have cardiac tamponade? JAMA. 2007;297(16):1810-1818.
Continuous, noninvasive measurement of pulsus paradoxus in patients with acute asthma. Arch Pediatr Adolesc Med. 1996;150(9):914-918. (authors not captured by the fetch tool; verify from PubMed)
Holleman DR Jr, Simel DL. Does the clinical examination predict airflow limitation? JAMA. 1995;273(4):313-319.
Pearson MG, Spence DP, Ryland I, Harrison BD. Value of pulsus paradoxus in assessing acute severe asthma. British Thoracic Society Standards of Care Committee. BMJ. 1993;307(6905):659.

safety_scope.do_not_use_when: Atrial fibrillation or very irregular rhythm, severe tachypnea, or when the patient cannot breathe quietly; do not use to exclude tamponade in patients with LV dysfunction, ASD, aortic regurgitation, or on positive-pressure ventilation.
safety_scope.escalation_warning: Pulsus >10 mmHg with hypotension, raised JVP and a known or suspected effusion is a tamponade emergency: immediate echo and preparation for pericardiocentesis.
safety_scope.interobserver_note: Manual measurement requires slow cuff deflation and is operator dependent; the RCE data derive from patients already selected for effusion/pericardiocentesis, which inflates apparent accuracy.

extraction_notes: Tamponade estimates from the JAMA RCE abstract (Roy 2007); the LR pair for >10 mmHg is from a single study within the review and the pooled sensitivity comes from 8 studies of patients already known to have tamponade (spectrum bias), so specificity is not available. The asthma RCE (Holleman & Simel 1995, source 2) has no abstract in PubMed and no PMC full text, so its pulsus figures could not be extracted; the BMJ 1993 adult asthma study (source 3) likewise has no abstract and PMC OA retrieval failed. The only quantified asthma estimate found is a pediatric ED study using continuous non-invasive measurement rather than a manual cuff; it is included with that caveat and should be weighted accordingly. Author names for source 1 were not returned by the fetch tool and are omitted; PMID/DOI confirmed.
